Subject: Your advice on senior analyst

Dear Noor,

You told me at the conference to read the criteria for the next level before planning anything. I finally did it last weekend, with my own record open beside it.

Four areas. Quality of analysis: I have plenty of evidence. Mentoring: two interns last year. Business impact: the churn model. But then: "Owns work that spans more than one team." Nothing. Everything I've done lives inside the risk team.

So I'm working backwards. If the review is in two quarters, I need a project by next month that makes that ownership visible. I'm proposing a shared dashboard with the collections team, where I own the data definitions for both groups. First milestone by March, full handover by June.

Would you look over the proposal before I send it?

Warmly,
Rehana

qa.q: Which criterion had no evidence in Rehana's record?
qa.a: "Owns work that spans more than one team."

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt on reaching the last criterion?
qa.a: Rehana was probably deflated at first, seeing nothing there, but then felt focused and determined once the gap gave a clear place to plan from.

qa.q: What else could Rehana do alongside working backward?
qa.a: Rehana could ask the manager directly whether the dashboard would count as cross-team ownership, so the plan is checked against how the criteria are actually judged.

qa.q: How might Noor see this email?
qa.a: Noor can see the advice was taken seriously, and may feel pleased and glad to help sharpen a plan that is already concrete.

You want to know how I got promoted, Dilnaz? It wasn't magic. It was a spreadsheet.
Last January I printed the senior-analyst criteria and put them next to my own work from the year. Five rows. Next to each I wrote what I had. Numbers accuracy, fine. Client reports, fine. Training juniors, fine. Then "leads initiatives across teams." I had written a big question mark.
That question mark bothered me all week. So I asked myself, what would count? And by when? The review was eight months away. I needed something that crossed teams and would show results by then.
I offered to run the shared forecasting process with the sales and supply teams. It took up two quarters of my life. But by the review, I had meeting notes, a process doc, and two team heads who'd seen me lead.
That's it. Pema's big secret: read the rubric first.

qa.q: How many rows did the criteria have?
How did Pema feel about the question mark next to "leads initiatives across teams"?
qa.a: Pema felt bothered and uneasy about it all week, which pushed Pema to work out what would count and plan backward.

qa.q: Which approach might suit Dilnaz if the criteria at Dilnaz's company are vague?
qa.a: Dilnaz could ask the manager directly for clear expectations and a timeline, since working backward only works when the target is written down.

qa.q: How might the sales and supply team heads see Pema's work?
qa.a: They saw Pema lead a process across their teams, so at review time they could speak for that cross-team ownership from their own experience.

grounding: It shows someone comparing senior-level criteria to their record, spotting the missing cross-team ownership and planning a project over two quarters to build it.
